extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / beginning graduate students in number theory and algebra (modular forms, Galois representations)
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture/notes covering topology preliminaries, Galois theory, representations, construction of Galois representations (cyclotomic and from elliptic curves), and the hypotheses/consequences of Serre's conjecture. Focuses on definitions, structural theorems, and key examples used to attach modular forms to Galois representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological Space (Definition 10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological space is a pair (X, T ) where X is a set and T ⊆ P(X) is a collection of subsets (the topology) such that: (1) ∅ ∈ T and X ∈ T; (2) arbitrary unions of elements of T are in T; (3) finite intersections of elements of T are in T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open sets are elements of T. Equivalent formulation via closed sets (swap unions/intersections). This formalises 'closeness' without a metric. Examples include open discs in C and the discrete topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subspace Topology (Definition 10.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (X, T) is a topological space and Y ⊆ X, the subspace topology on Y is TY = {U ∩ Y | U ∈ T}. A set V ⊆ Y is open in Y iff there exists U open in X with V = U ∩ Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to restrict topologies to subsets; the pair (Y, TY) is called a subspace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basis for a Topology (Definition 10.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A collection B of subsets of X is a basis if: (1) for each x ∈ X there exists B ∈ B with x ∈ B; (2) if x ∈ B1 ∩ B2 (B1,B2∈B) then there exists B3 ∈ B with x ∈ B3 ⊆ B1 ∩ B2. The topology generated by B has open sets which are unions of basis elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This abstracts the role played by open balls/discs; every open set is a union of basis elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product Topology (finite) (Definition 10.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given (X, TX) and (Y, TY), the product topology TX×Y is generated by the basis B = {U×V | U∈TX, V∈TY}. W ⊆ X×Y is open iff for each (x,y)∈W there exist U,V open with (x,y)∈U×V ⊆ W.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The product topology makes canonical projections continuous and captures 'coordinate-wise' openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product Topology (infinite) (Definition 10.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a family {(Xi, Ti)}i∈I, the product topology on ∏i∈I Xi is generated by basic opens ∏i Ui where Ui ∈ Ti and Ui = Xi for all but finitely many i. It is the coarsest topology making all projection maps continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic open sets vary in finitely many coordinates only. This is the standard topology used for inverse limits and Krull topology constructions later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous Function (Definition 10.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: f : X → Y between topological spaces is continuous if for every open V ⊆ Y the preimage f^{-1}(V) belongs to TX; equivalently the preimage of every open set is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalises the ε-δ definition; in discrete topology every function is continuous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete Topology (Example 10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discrete topology on X is the power set P(X); every subset is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a trivial topology making every function from X continuous; useful example and extremal case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological Group (Definition 10.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A topological group is a group G with a topology such that the multiplication µ: G×G→G and inversion ι: G→G are continuous (with G×G having the product topology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For topological groups a neighbourhood base at the identity often suffices to describe topology; analogous definitions apply to topological rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field Extension (Definition 10.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: K is a field extension of F (written K/F) if F ⊆ K and the operations of F are those of K restricted to F. K is an F-vector space; the extension is finite if this vector space is finite-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic concept underpinning Galois theory; 'finite' is a key finiteness condition used throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aut(K/F) (Definition 10.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aut(K/F) is the group of field automorphisms of K that fix every element of F: Aut(K/F) = {σ ∈ Aut(K) | σ(f)=f ∀ f∈F}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When K/F is Galois, this group is denoted Gal(K/F) and forms the central object of study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galois Extension (Definition 10.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension E/F is Galois if it is normal and separable: normal means every irreducible polynomial in F[x] with a root in E splits completely in E; separable means minimal polynomials have no repeated roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galois extensions are precisely those to which the Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory applies; separability holds automatically over fields of characteristic 0 and finite fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Galois Theory (Theorem 10.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite Galois extension E/F with G = Gal(E/F), there is a one-to-one inclusion-reversing correspondence between intermediate fields F ⊆ K ⊆ E and subgroups H ≤ G given by K ↦ Gal(E/K) and H ↦ E^H (fixed field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: K normal over F ⇔ corresponding H normal in G; in that case Gal(K/F) ≅ G/H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic Closure (Definition 10.11) and Proposition 10.1
rubrics_metrics.description: The algebraic closure K̄ of a field K is the smallest field extension containing roots of all polynomials over K. Proposition: For char 0, the algebraic closure is a Galois extension (separable + normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algebraic closures provide the ambient field in which absolute Galois groups are defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frobenius Automorphism in Finite Fields (Definition 10.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: In F_{p^k}, the Frobenius element Frob_p is x ↦ x^p. It is an automorphism fixing F_p and gives the generator of Gal(F_{q^n}/F_q) in classification theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties include Frob_p(a+b) = a^p + b^p and multiplicativity; Fermat's little theorem shows it fixes F_p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Finite Field Extensions (Theorem 10.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For F_q with q = p^r: for each n≥1 there is a unique (up to iso) extension F_{q^n}; F_{q^n}/F_q is Galois of degree n with cyclic Galois group generated by Frobenius; intermediate fields correspond to divisors of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful concrete model for Galois theory; lattices of subfields correspond to subgroup structure of Z/nZ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group Representation (Definition 10.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation of a group G on a vector space V over field F is a group homomorphism ρ: G → GL(V). For dim V = 2 and chosen basis one views ρ as G → GL2(F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects abstract groups to linear/algebraic objects and is the language for Galois representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducible Representation (Definition 10.14)
rubrics_metrics.description: A representation ρ: G → GL(V) is irreducible if the only G-invariant subspaces of V are {0} and V itself (i.e., no proper nontrivial invariant subspaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent formulations are useful in 2-dim cases and are used as hypotheses in modularity/Serre statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute Galois Group and Krull Topology (Definitions 11.1–11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: G_Q = Gal(Q̄/Q) = Aut(Q̄). View G_Q as inverse limit of finite Galois groups Gal(K/Q) with restriction maps; give each finite group discrete topology and the inverse limit the subspace topology of the product (Krull topology). The collection {Gal(Q̄/K) | K/Q finite Galois} forms a basis of open neighbourhoods of identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This makes G_Q a profinite topological group; topology is essential for defining continuous Galois representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galois Representation of G_Q (Definition 11.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Galois representation of G_Q is a continuous group homomorphism ρ: Gal(Q̄/Q) → GL_n(R) where R is a topological ring (commonly Q_ℓ, Z_ℓ, O_F, or a finite field), GL_n(R) has topology from R, Gal(Q̄/Q) has the Krull topology, and ρ is continuous. For the notes n = 2 is the primary case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity is crucial; choices of R give rise to mod ℓ, ℓ-adic, or p-adic representations and influence arithmetic properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mod ℓ and ℓ-adic Galois Representations (Definitions 11.5–11.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mod ℓ representation is a continuous homomorphism ρ̄: G_Q → GL_n(F_ℓ) (GL_n(F_ℓ) discrete). An ℓ-adic representation is ρ: G_Q → GL_n(Q_ℓ) (or finite extension), continuous w.r.t. Krull topology and ℓ-adic topology on GL_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ℓ-adic reps often arise as inverse limits of compatible mod ℓ^n representations; reduction modulo ℓ relates ℓ-adic and mod ℓ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity ⇒ factors through finite quotient for finite target (Proposition 11.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ρ: G_Q → GL2(F_q) with F_q finite (discrete topology), then ρ factors through some finite quotient Gal(K/Q) for a finite Galois extension K/Q: G_Q ↠ Gal(K/Q) → GL2(F_q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because preimage of identity is an open neighbourhood of identity, it contains Gal(Q̄/K) for some finite K, forcing factorisation. Similar for Z/ℓ^nZ targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cyclotomic Characters (Definitions 11.7 and 11.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For p and k, the mod-p^k cyclotomic character χ_{p^k}: G_Q → GL1(Z/p^kZ) records action on p^k-th roots of unity. The p-adic cyclotomic character χ: G_Q → GL1(Z_p) is the inverse limit of these; χ(σ) = (χ_{p^0}(σ), χ_{p^1}(σ), ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction requires compatible choices of primitive roots; independence of primitive root choice is proved; χ is a 1-dimensional p-adic representation and plays role of determinant in many arithmetic representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oddness of 2-dim mod ℓ representations (Definition 11.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-dimensional mod ℓ representation ρ: G_Q → GL2(F_ℓ) is odd if det ρ(c) = −1 where c is complex conjugation (c(x+iy)=x−iy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oddness (determinant −1 at complex conjugation) is a necessary condition for arising from modular forms; even corresponds to +1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreducibility criterion for 2-dimensional mod ℓ representations (Proposition 11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: ρ: G_Q → GL2(F_ℓ) is irreducible iff there is no v ∈ F_ℓ^2 which is simultaneously an eigenvector of ρ(σ) for all σ∈G_Q; equivalently there is no B ∈ GL2(F_ℓ) making all ρ(σ) upper-triangular with zero bottom-left entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete criterion is often used to check irreducibility in practice for 2-dim reps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serre's conjecture (assumptions and conclusion) (Theorems 11.2 and 11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any odd, irreducible 2-dimensional mod p Galois representation ρ: G_Q → GL2(F_p) is modular: there exist natural invariants N, k, ε (level, weight, nebentypus) and a cusp form f of weight k and level N such that for primes ℓ ∤ Np, ρ is unramified at ℓ and Tr(Frob_ℓ | ρ) = a_ℓ (Fourier coefficient) and det(Frob_ℓ | ρ) = ε(ℓ) ℓ^{k−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem is stated with emphasis on minimal hypotheses (odd, irreducible); associating the invariants N,k,ε to ρ is central to Serre's recipe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galois representations from elliptic curves (Definitions 11.10–11.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an elliptic curve E/Q, for each n the action of G_Q on E[n] (n-torsion) yields ρ_{E,n}: G_Q → Aut(E[n]) ≅ GL2(Z/nZ). Taking inverse limit over ℓ^n gives the ℓ-adic Tate module representation ρ_{E,ℓ}: G_Q → GL2(Z_ℓ) ⊂ GL2(Q_ℓ). Reducing gives mod ℓ representation on E[ℓ].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemmas show σ permutes torsion points, is additive on torsion, and action factors compatibly through Tate module. These representations are the primary geometric sources of Galois reps used in modularity problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key propositions relating elliptic-curve reps and Serre's hypotheses (Props 11.4–11.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposition: For Frey curve of x^P + y^P = z^P and P≥5, the mod P representation ρ_{E,P} is irreducible. If ρ is irreducible then det ρ = χ (cyclotomic). If det ρ = χ then ρ is odd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts are used in the proof strategies linking Frey curves, modularity, and Fermat's Last Theorem (Wiles-style arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting zeros via modified argument principle (complex-analytic step earlier)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count zeros of a modular form inside a specially constructed path γ (decomposed into segments γ1..γ6 and small detours) use the argument principle modified by SL_2(Z): integrals (1/2πi) ∮_γ f'(z)/f(z) dz around segments equal multiplicities of zeros at cusps/elliptic points or multiplicity in q-expansions (denoted ν_∞(f), ν_{1+i/2}(f) etc). By arranging arcs small and choosing imaginary parts large, integrals concentrate to quarter-turn contributions (e.g., π/2 → 1/4) and to q-expansion multiplicities at cusps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to deduce contradictions (e.g., no non-zero cusp forms of weight 2 over Γ_0(2)) by summing contributions and comparing to cusp-form vanishing at infinity (ν_∞(f)≥1). The method explains how local multiplicities (zeros at elliptic points and cusps) are computed via contour integrals and q-expansion orders.
